books.section: Topic 7.3 The Spanish-American War and Its Aftermath

primary_sources: President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898

stimulus.source_note: President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898, public domain (abridged).
stimulus.text: "First. In the cause of humanity and to put an end to the barbarities, bloodshed, starvation, and horrible miseries now existing there, and which the parties to the conflict are either unable or unwilling to stop or mitigate. It is no answer to say this is all in another country, belonging to another nation, and is therefore none of our business. It is specially our duty, for it is right at our door. Second. We owe it to our citizens in Cuba to afford them that protection and indemnity for life and property which no government there can or will afford. . . . Third. The right to intervene may be justified by the very serious injury to the commerce, trade, and business of our people, and by the wanton destruction of property and devastation of the island." — President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim abridged excerpt from President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898, public domain
stem: In his message, McKinley's first reason for intervention is

options.misconception: McKinley never asks to annex Cuba; he asks Congress to authorize measures to end the war there.

options.text: To punish Spain for sinking the Maine
options.misconception: McKinley never blames Spain for the Maine in this passage; his first reason is Cuban suffering.

options.text: To end the suffering of Cubans

options.misconception: The Philippines are not mentioned in this passage; McKinley's message is about Cuba.

rationales.A: Annexation is nowhere in the message. McKinley asks for measures to end the fighting in Cuba.
rationales.B: The Maine goes unmentioned in these reasons. The first reason is the suffering in Cuba itself.
rationales.C: McKinley's first reason is humanity: to end the barbarities, bloodshed, starvation, and miseries in Cuba.
rationales.D: The message is about Cuba. Background: the Philippines enter the war later, through Dewey's victory at Manila Bay.
rationales.general:
1. Find the list. McKinley numbers his reasons: first, second, third.
2. Read the first. He puts humanity first: ending the barbarities, bloodshed, and starvation in Cuba.
3. Check the rest. Annexation, the Maine, and the Philippines never appear as reasons here.
Remember: when a writer numbers reasons, the order is part of the argument, so read them in order.
